info.bio:
Blondie emergió de la escena underground de Nueva York de fines de los 70, y logró hacer realmente masivo el sonido que provenía del punk, encabezando la movida más estilizada de esa vertiente que la prensa llamaría new wave. 

La banda encontró una indeleble marca registrada en la imagen y actitud de su cantante, la magnética Debbie Harry y a nivel musical se permitió coquetear con gracia entre distintos ritmos como el punk, el glam rock, el sonido de grupos de los 60 como The Ronettes, y la música disco.

scenes.name: Downtown: graffiti, punk y hip hop en el Mudd Club, Negril y el Roxy
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Fab 5 Freddy (Fred Brathwaite), del grupo de grafiteros de Brooklyn Fabulous 5 con Lee Quiñones, ofrecía en The Village Voice murales por encargo; con Michael Holman montó la Canal Zone Party (1979), donde apareció Jean-Michel Basquiat, mitad de SAMO, y llevó a Bambaataa al Mudd Club. La Zulu Nation y los Funky 4 + 1, que mezclaban punk y hip hop ante los Beastie Boys, bajaron al Ritz, el Mudd Club, Danceteria, Negril y el Roxy de Kool Lady Blue: en Negril, cedido por el mánager de los Clash, se juntaron por primera vez los cuatro elementos; en el Roxy, una pista de patinaje de la calle 18, Bambaataa, Afrika Islam y Grand Mixer D.ST pinchaban para Bianca Jagger, Warhol, la Rock Steady Crew o Madonna. Debbie Harry y Chris Stein (Blondie), amigos de Flash, nombraron a Freddy y a Flash en «Rapture» (1981), primer rap número 1 en Billboard, y llevaron a los Funky 4 + 1 a Saturday Night Live (14 de febrero de 1981), primera actuación de hip hop en la televisión nacional. Para Holman, sin el abrazo del downtown el hip hop no habría sido lo que fue; para Dante Ross, los negros se llevaron pantalones pitillo y opiáceos y los blancos toda esa cultura.
scenes.family: Cultura hip hop: graffiti, baile, cine, moda, política

scenes.name: Punk neoyorquino del CBGB
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Ramones, Television, Patti Smith, Blondie, The Heartbreakers: una escena que, como advirtió James Wolcott en 1975 («Un impulso conservador en el nuevo underground del rock»), se presentaba como el retorno de algo perdido. Los Ramones agotan su idea en dos discos, los Heartbreakers son Dr. Feelgood con heroína y hasta Television bebe del acid rock de la costa oeste. La revista Punk de Legs McNeil proclama «¡Muerte a esa mierda disco!» y rechaza al hipster como «negro blanco».
scenes.family: Antecedentes: punk, art rock, kraut y glam

scenes.name: Club 57, Mudd Club y el arte del downtown
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Dos clubes rivales como laboratorios artísticos. El Club 57, en el sótano de una iglesia polaca, era «groovy»: fiestas temáticas de Ann Magnuson, Kenny Scharf, Keith Haring y John Sex, camp, travestismo y psicodelia, con Klaus Nomi y la anti-banda Pulsallama. El Mudd Club de Steve Maas era «cool»: decadencia no wave, metacualona y heroína, el «Funeral del rock'n'roll» y la fiesta del soul de Michael Holman. Allí tocaba Gray, el grupo de ruido de Jean-Michel Basquiat, Holman y Vincent Gallo; Basquiat produjo «Beat Bop» de Rammellzee y el downtown abrazó el grafiti y el hip hop. El boom de las galerías (FUN, Times Square Show, New York/New Wave), la llegada de Reagan, la «Operation Pressure Point» de Giuliani y el sida acabaron con el diletantismo: «era cuestión de crear o morir».
scenes.family: Nueva York: no wave y mutant disco

scenes.name: Música de baile para punks
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La disco y el punk florecen a la vez y acaban fusionándose, pese a representar valores casi opuestos. Blondie define la fusión de hedonismo disco y estética punk; Madonna es el híbrido definitivo y redefine la balada de rhythm'n'blues para la era de los ritmos electrónicos. Las mujeres llevan la actitud punk a las discotecas. Talking Heads asimilan el funk en la canción new wave y, con Eno, llegan a la fusión de futurismo y primitivismo de Remain In Light; Byrne y Eno firman My Life In The Bush Of Ghosts. ESG, Liquid Liquid, Defunkt, Bush Tetras, los Contortions de James Chance (Albert Ayler + Beefheart + James Brown), la Love Of Life Orchestra de Peter Gordon, Suburbs, Was Not Was, Wall Of Voodoo.
scenes.family: Soul, funk, disco, hip hop y baile

scenes.name: Hip hop old school
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: El MC es la figura central: un collage de ritmos y ruidos como base para una nueva poesía urbana.
scenes.family: Hip hop, breaks y ritmo lento

scenes.name: New wave americana
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: La new wave culta, sin prejuicios raciales, abre la puerta al dub y los ritmos negros: Devo y su «devolución» kraftwerkiana; Blondie, que coquetea con la disco y con Moroder; Talking Heads y sus sonidos de raíz; los B-52’s psicotrónicos; y el reverso maldito de San Francisco, Tuxedomoon y The Residents.

podcast.body: Blondie was formed around 1975 and quickly became part of the punk and art rock scene centered at CBGB. "Blondie was part of the punk and art rock scene at CBGB starting in about 1975."

podcast.title: Prominent Band in New York Scene (1975)
podcast.body: Blondie was identified as one of the leading bands in the emerging New York music scene in 1975, a movement centered around the legendary CBGB club. "En Nueva York estaban emergiendo una escena liderada por bandas como Ramones, Televisión, Patie Smith, Suicide, Blondie or Tolkien Hets."

podcast.title: CBGB Staple (1978)
podcast.body: By 1978, Blondie was a staple at CBGB in New York and accepted by all the punks. While their music was not purely punk, it could not have been created without punk's prior existence, as it adopted the correct attitude and approach but introduced additional elements that defined the New Wave sound. "By 1978, was a staple at CBGB in New York, they were accepted by all the punks."

podcast.title: Exploration of Hip-Hop with Fab 5 Freddy (1978)
podcast.body: In 1978, Debbie Harry and Chris Stein were introduced to the emerging hip-hop scene in the Bronx by Fred Brathwaite, also known as Fab 5 Freddy, whom they met at CBGB. Freddy saw a synergy between the downtown punk and uptown hip-hop scenes, leading Harry and Stein to experiment with rap, starting with an unreleased Christmas record and culminating in "Rapture." "The story goes that in 1978, Debbie Harry and Chris Stein were taken by Fred Brathwaite, better known in hip-hop circles as Fab5 Freddie. Up to the Bronx, where they witnessed their first rap show..."

podcast.body: After a couple of years of hard work following their formation, Blondie became one of the biggest bands in the world, with their breakthrough record released in 1978. "And after a couple of years of very hard work, Blondie became one of the biggest bands in the world."

podcast.title: Quad-fecta of Number One Hits (1979-1981)
podcast.body: Blondie achieved four number one songs between the spring of 1979 and the winter of 1981, each in a distinctly different style or genre: disco ("Heart of Glass"), electro rock ("Call Me"), reggae ("The Tide Is High"), and hip-hop ("Rapture"). This demonstrated their remarkable versatility and commercial appeal during their "imperial era." "Completing Blondie's quad-fecta of number one songs all scored between the spring of 1979 and the winter of 1981 and in four different styles."

podcast.title: Collaborations with Giorgio Moroder (1980)
podcast.body: Debbie Harry was invited to contribute to the soundtrack of Paul Schrader's 1980 film *American Gigolo*. The film's score was overseen by Italian producer Giorgio Moroder, known for his work with Donna Summer and his Oscar-winning score for *Midnight Express*. Moroder was seen as an ideal producer to steer Blondie towards electronic music and danceable rock, leading to the creation of "Call Me." "This made Moroder, perhaps the ideal producer to push Blondie further in the direction of electronic music and danceable rock."

podcast.title: Debbie Harry's Celebrity Status (1980-1981)
podcast.body: During the recording of *Autoamerican*, Debbie Harry's prominence grew significantly. She was invited as a showcase guest on an episode of "The Muppet Show" and Blondie was approached to contribute a theme song for the James Bond film *For Your Eyes Only*. Harry also recorded a solo album during this period, indicating her rising individual stardom. "Debbie Harry was invited to be the showcase guest on an episode of The Muppet Show."

podcast.title: Transition to New Wave Era (1980)
podcast.body: At the start of the 1980s, Blondie was among several bands attempting to expand the definition of punk to achieve pop chart success. Their single "Atomic" in early 1980 was key in pointing a way forward for them in the new wave era, blending surf rock, cowboy twang, and danceable rock elements. "What was most important about Atomic was how it pointed away forward for Blondie in the new wave era."

podcast.title: First Solo Album - KooKoo (1981)
podcast.body: Debbie Harry recorded her solo debut album, *KooKoo*, in the first half of 1981 with Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards of the disco supergroup Chic. The album moved her further into "Black informed pop," featuring cutting-edge music like the dance hit "Backfire" and the breakbeat track "The Jam Was Moving." The album cover, an image by sci-fi/horror artist H.R. Giger depicting her face pierced with swords, was noted as "freaky." Despite its artistic ambition, *KooKoo* was not a commercial success, peaking at number 25 on the album chart, producing no Top 40 hits, and exiting the chart within three months. "It was the first sign that Blondie's imperial era was coming to a close."

podcast.title: Prolonged Hiatus (1983-1997)
podcast.body: Following the commercial disappointment of *The Hunter* in 1982 and the end of their Chrysalis Records contract, Blondie went on a prolonged hiatus by 1983. Debbie Harry then resumed her solo career, even recording a single for the Al Pacino film *Scarface*, and did not return to the group for over a decade and a half. "By 1983, Blondie had gone on a prolonged hiatus."

podcast.title: Clem Burke Death (2025) – Cancer Kept Secret
podcast.body: Clem Burke, original drummer of Blondie, died in 2025 of cancer, which had been kept secret. He briefly played with the Ramones under the name Elvis Ramone. He also participated in an eight-year academic study on the physical and psychological effects of being a professional drummer, for which he received an honorary doctorate in music. "His cancer was kept secret."

podcast.title: "Debbie Blondie" Nickname
podcast.body: In an effort to distinguish her solo career from the band, Debbie Harry jokingly noted that fans sometimes called her "Debbie Blondie" or mistakenly assumed the group's name referred solely to her. This illustrates her strong identification with the band's image. "Debbie Harry joked at the time that fans sometimes called her Debbie Blondie or just assumed the group's name meant her."

podcast.body: The band's name, Blondie, was an homage to the "cat calls" Debbie Harry frequently received while walking through the streets of New York City. "The band name was an homage to the cat calls that Debbie Harry got as she walked through the streets of New York."

podcast.title: Biggest Selling American New Wave Band
podcast.body: By 1983, Blondie, alongside Talking Heads, had become one of the biggest selling American New Wave bands. Their success marked a significant crossover from their punk roots into the mainstream. "The Talking Hits from 1983, and along with Blondie, they became the biggest selling American New Wave bands."

podcast.title: CBGB Relationship
podcast.body: Blondie had a "love-hate relationship" with CBGB; Debbie Harry described it as a "dark and smelly" place infested with rats and flies, but its proximity to her home (five or six blocks away) made it a convenient venue for regular performances. She wasn't fully aware of being part of a "movement" at the time, and found it hard to concentrate in the disgusting environment. "Blondie had a love-hate relationship with CBGB. It was dark and smelly with rats and flies on one hand, but it was five or six blocks from home and the band could play there on the other hand."

podcast.body: Burke briefly filled in as drummer for the Ramones under the name "Elvis Ramone." He was also the subject of an eight-year university study examining the physical and psychological demands placed on professional rock drummers, resulting in an honorary doctorate in music. "Participated in an eight-year study on the physical and psychological effects of being a professional drummer, receiving an honorary doctorate in music."

podcast.body: Debbie Harry first encountered John Holt's "The Tide Is High" on a compilation tape she acquired in London, which directly inspired Blondie's decision to record their highly successful cover version. "Debbie Harry heard that song on a compilation tape that she got in London, London and decided that she had to record it."

podcast.title: Early Scene Development
podcast.body: Clem Burke, Blondie's drummer, noted that much of the band's early development happened "by accident." He viewed the insular New York scene as an opportunity for bands, comprising about 100 people (85 in bands), to make mistakes publicly and learn. He considered CBGB their version of "the Cavern where the Beatles started." "Crucially, we could make mistakes in public, finding our way at those early shows. Even at the time I saw CBGB's club as our version of the cavern where the Beatles started."

podcast.title: Studio Challenges with Mike Chapman
podcast.body: Producer Mike Chapman described Blondie as "tough in the studio," citing significant animosity among members (except for Chris Stein and Debbie Harry). He found them "juvenile in their approach to life," prioritizing fun over hard work. Debbie Harry admitted Chapman "drove me crazy" but also credited him with teaching her to "listen more carefully." "He said the Blondies, as he called them, were tough in the studio, real tough. None of them liked each other except Chris and Debbie and there was so much animosity. They were really, really juvenile in their approach to life. A classic New York underground rock band and they didn't give a fuck about anything. They just wanted to have fun and didn't want to work too hard getting it."

xref.title: Friends with Blondie and Ramones; Almost Signed to IRS; Influenced B-52s; Background Vocals on Blondie's Autoamerican
xref.body: The B-Girls formed in Toronto in 1977 with a sound closer to British Invasion mid-1960s than hard punk, though their look and attitude were fully punk. They toured with and opened for Teenage Head, the Viletones, and eventually The Clash, then relocated to New York where they became close with Blondie, the Ramones, the Cramps, and the Dead Boys. Members sang background vocals on Blondie's *Autoamerican* (1980), had demos produced by Debbie Harry and Mick Jones of The Clash, and nearly signed with IRS Records — which chose a Los Angeles band called the Go-Go's instead. The Go-Go's were fans of the B-Girls. The B-Girls' existence and sound also influenced a band from Georgia called the B-52s. No album was released before the original lineup fell apart by 1981. "This Canadian punk band influenced not just Blondie and the Go-Go's, but a band visiting New York from Georgia called the B-52s."

xref.body: All members of Franz Ferdinand admired the spiky, jittery, stop-start music of the 1970s, citing influences from Joy Division, The Fall, Blondie, The Stranglers, and Gang of Four. Their music managed to sound fresh despite being inspired by these earlier sounds. "Everybody in the band had a fondness for that spiky, jittery, stop-start stuff in the 1970s. Joy Division in the fall, Blondie, the Stranglers, Gang of Four."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

xref.title: Musical Style
xref.body: The band specialized in short, sharp, choppy songs, characterized by a prominent use of rhythm guitar and a vaguely anti-corporate stance. This style was shared with other New Wave artists like Blondie and Elvis Costello. "like the talking heads and blondie and Elvis Costello, Tom Petty specialized in short, sharp choppy songs with lots of rhythm guitar and vaguely anti-corporate stents."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

xref.title: Musical Style
xref.body: Elvis Costello specialized in short, sharp, choppy songs, featuring a significant amount of rhythm guitar and a vaguely anti-corporate stance. This musical approach was similar to that of Talking Heads, Blondie, and Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, all of whom were categorized under the New Wave banner. "like the talking heads and blondie and Elvis Costello, Tom Petty specialized in short, sharp choppy songs with lots of rhythm guitar and vaguely anti-corporate stents."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

xref.title: New Wave Artist
xref.body: Elvis Costello was identified as a New Wave artist, grouped alongside bands such as Talking Heads, Blondie, and Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, indicating his contribution to the evolving sound of modern rock. "The talking heads and blondie and Elvis Costello were new wave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

xref.title: New Wave Branding
xref.body: Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, a relatively new band from Florida, were categorized as New Wave. This classification was based on their shared musical characteristics with other New Wave acts like Talking Heads, Blondie, and Elvis Costello. "And so as this new band from Florida called Tom Petty in the Heartbreakers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6

xref.title: New York Punk and Apolitical Stance
xref.body: Originating in New York, the Ramones were part of the early punk scene, which catered to artsy outsiders. While there was some general rebellion, the Ramones, alongside other major players like Blondie and the Talking Heads, were not notably political in their musical output. "if you look at the major players, like the Ramones and Blondie and the Talking Heds, none of them were very political."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Songs of Protest

xref.title: New York Punk and Apolitical Stance
xref.body: The Talking Heads were part of the artsy outsider punk movement in New York. Along with bands like the Ramones and Blondie, they were generally not characterized by political songwriting, setting them apart from their British punk counterparts. "if you look at the major players, like the Ramones and Blondie and the Talking Heds, none of them were very political."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Songs of Protest

xref.title: Performance During CBGB's Final Weeks
xref.body: Bad Brains was one of the bands that performed at CBGB during its final weeks leading up to its closure in October 2006. "The final weeks featured bands like Bad Brains, The Dictators, and even Blondie."

xref.body: The Ramones were cited as one of the bands, alongside the Sex Pistols and Blondie, that initiated the "new music scene." "It started with bands like the Ramones and the Sex Pistols and Blondie."

xref.title: Presence in CBGB Scene
xref.body: The Talking Heads were among the significant bands that emerged from and helped define the scene at CBGB in the 1970s. "The Ramones, the talking heads, blondie, television, and so many hundreds of other groups turned this dive bar into a scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: Television was one of the many groups that were integral to the punk rock scene that developed at CBGB in the 1970s. "The Ramones, the talking heads, blondie, television, and so many hundreds of other groups turned this dive bar into a scene."

xref.title: Prominent New Wave Artist
xref.body: The Police were recognized as one of the artists who rode "the crest of New Wave." Their commercial success and distinct sound helped to define the diverse and more commercially viable landscape of New Wave music. "And running the crest of New Wave, who artists like the police, Elvis Costello, Blondie, Devo, and The Talking Hits."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Prominent New Wave and Power Pop Artist
xref.body: Elvis Costello was highlighted as an artist running "the crest of New Wave" and was also cited as an example of a Power Pop artist, which was one of the many subgenres encompassed by the broader New Wave movement. "And running the crest of New Wave, who artists like the police, Elvis Costello, Blondie, Devo, and The Talking Hits."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Etymology: Part 1

xref.title: Radio Success
xref.body: The Pretenders were among the New Wave bands that found success on pop and rock radio, indicating their ability to cross over to mainstream audiences. "While some New Wave bands thrived on pop and rock radio, the pretenders, blondie, the cars, the police, among them, others struggled to find attention outside of their original circle of fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: The Police were one of the New Wave bands that successfully gained traction on pop and rock radio, contributing to the genre's broader appeal. xref.title: Record Deal and Distribution
xref.body: Patti Smith was one of the artists from the burgeoning New York scene who secured a record deal, enabling her music to be distributed and heard beyond New York City. "Eventually, word gets out and groups like the Ramones and the Talking Heads and television in Blondie and Patty Smith get record deals and their music begins to be distributed beyond New York."

xref.title: Television Spin-off and CBGB Scene Involvement
xref.body: The Heartbreakers were identified as a "television spin-off band" and were part of the burgeoning CBGB scene, alongside Blondie, Suicide, and The Talking Heads, as the club became a central hub for new music.
